# Introduction

This report examines a central question in collaboration network research: what mechanisms determine whether an individual becomes a “star” performer? Using a large scale dataset of researchers containing measures of scientific impact, collaboration structure, elite tie quality, and knowledge breadth, the analysis investigates how network position and expertise shape performance outcomes. The study is grounded in three complementary theoretical perspectives: learning from high performing collaborators (Liu et al., 2018), brokerage advantages arising from structural holes (Burt, 2004), and the T shaped model of deep–broad knowledge integration (Fleming, 2001). 

These frameworks motivate an empirical assessment of whether elite collaboration exerts an independent influence on performance after accounting for productivity, network cohesion, and expertise diversity. To address this question, the report integrates exploratory data analysis with regression modelling, LASSO regularisation, and classification techniques to provide a multi angle evaluation of the drivers of star performance.


```{r load-data}

df <- read_csv(DATA_PATH, show_col_types = FALSE)

### check summary of data
summary(df)

### remove zero(0) from AID which has extreme value compared to 2nd max value
df <- df[df$AID != 0, ]

cat("Dataset:", nrow(df), "observations,", ncol(df), "columns\n")

    sprintf("(%.1f%%)\n", 100 * mean(df$Is_HighPerformer)))


```

# Methodology

The analysis follows a structured, theory‑aligned pipeline designed to identify the network mechanisms that differentiate star performers. Missing values were handled using a dual strategy: elite‑collaboration variables exhibited ~80% structural missingness due to the absence of elite partners, so zeros were imputed and a binary indicator captured this condition. Variables with low missingness (2–7%) were median‑imputed to preserve distributional properties without distorting variance. The full dataset was retained without sampling, consistent with guidance for large‑scale collaboration networks, ensuring that rare elite‑interaction patterns were not lost.

Total_Impact was log‑transformed after verifying extreme right‑skewness; this stabilised variance and allowed linear models to capture proportional rather than absolute differences in scientific influence. The modelling pipeline integrates multiple linear regression, polynomial regression, LASSO regularisation, logistic regression, and LDA. LASSO was evaluated through a coefficient‑path plot and variable‑selection table at the optimal λ, and its selected predictors were compared with forward selection to assess model stability. Predictive models were trained using a 70/30 train–test split with a fixed random seed to ensure reproducibility and fair evaluation under severe class imbalance.

# Part 1: Exploratory Data Analysis

## Summary Statistics


```{r q1-summary}

cat("Dataset:", nrow(df), "observations,", ncol(df), "columns\n")


# ================================
#  Define Variables
# ================================
key_vars <- c("Total_Impact", "Total_Projects", "Career_Length",
              "Num_Elite_Collaborators", "Num_Regular_Collaborators",
              "Network_Constraint", "Effective_Size")

# ================================
#  Check Missing Columns (Safety Check)
# ================================
missing_cols <- setdiff(key_vars, names(df))
if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
  stop(paste("These columns are missing in df:", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", ")))
}

# ================================
# Summary Statistics Table
# ================================
summary_tbl <- df %>%
  select(all_of(key_vars)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(),
               names_to = "Variable",
               values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(
    N        = sum(!is.na(value)),
    Mean     = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD       = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min      = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q1       = quantile(value, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median   = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q3       = quantile(value, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max      = max(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    Missing  = sum(is.na(value)),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = key_vars)) %>%
  arrange(Variable)

# Print formatted table
summary_tbl %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Q1: Summary Statistics for Key Variables") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE)

# ================================
#  NA Statistics for ALL Variables
# ================================
na_stats <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(df),
  NA_Count = sapply(df, function(x) sum(is.na(x))),
  NA_Percentage = sapply(df, function(x) {
    sum(is.na(x)) / length(x) * 100
  })
)

# Sort by highest NA %
na_stats <- na_stats %>%
  arrange(desc(NA_Percentage))

print(na_stats)


```

## Handling Imputations for NA and Zeros

```{r Handling Imputations for NA and Zeros}

### creating new variable to show has elite or not 
df$Has_Elite <- ifelse(is.na(df$Cohesion_Elite), 0, 1)

vars_elite <- c("Cohesion_Elite", "Expertise_Sim_Elite", "Repeated_Elite")

# move zero(0) since there is no start performer present
df[vars_elite] <- lapply(df[vars_elite], function(x) {
  x[is.na(x)] <- 0
  return(x)
})

# Median imputation
vars_med <- c("Network_Constraint", "Cohesion_Regular", 
              "Expertise_Sim_Regular", "Repeated_Regular",
              "Effective_Size", "Network_Efficiency")

for (col in vars_med) {
  df[[col]][is.na(df[[col]])] <- median(df[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
}

# ================================
# Transform variables
# ================================
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    Log_Impact = log1p(Total_Impact),
    log_Num_Elite = log1p(Num_Elite_Collaborators),
    log_Effective_Size = log1p(Effective_Size)
  )

### check the NAs after imputation
cat("Missing values per variable:\n")
colSums(is.na(df)) %>% .[. > 0]
```

## Scatter Plots

```{r q3-scatter, fig.width=16, fig.height=5}

# ---- 1. Sample 5% of data (fastest + visually identical) ----

df_small <- df %>% sample_frac(0.05)

# ---- 2. Prepare transformed variables ----
scatter_scaled <- df_small %>%
  transmute(
    Log_Impact,
    log_Num_Elite = log1p(Num_Elite_Collaborators),
    Cohesion_Elite,
    log_Effective_Size = log1p(Effective_Size)
  ) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = -Log_Impact,
    names_to = "Predictor",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) %>%
  tidyr::drop_na()

# ---- 3. Fast GAM-based scatterplots ----
ggplot(scatter_scaled, aes(Value, Log_Impact)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "gam",
    formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"),
    colour = "red",
    linewidth = 1,
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Predictor, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Exploratory Scaled Scatter Plots",
    subtitle = "Using 5% sample + GAM smoothing for fast, stable visualisation",
    x = NULL,
    y = "log(Total Impact + 1)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

## Interpretation: Exploratory Data Analysis

The exploratory analysis began with summary statistics for key performance and network variables, including Total_Impact, Total_Projects, Career_Length, Num_Elite_Collaborators, Num_Regular_Collaborators, Network_Constraint, and Effective_Size. These variables exhibited substantial right‑skewness, particularly Total_Impact and elite‑collaboration counts, motivating the use of log‑transformations to stabilize variance and reveal underlying functional relationships. The correlation heatmap revealed several highly correlated variable pairs (|r| > 0.7), particularly among network size and collaboration measures. To mitigate multicollinearity, only representative variables from each group were retained for modelling. 

To visualize functional patterns, scatterplots were generated using a 5% random sample (~26k observations) combined with GAM smoothing, which preserved the underlying relationships while avoiding overplotting. The relationships with Log_Impact varied in shape: log‑transformed Effective_Size displayed an almost linear trend; Cohesion_Elite showed a weak, curved pattern; and log(Num_Elite + 1) exhibited a strong non‑linear effect, rising steeply at low elite exposure and plateauing at higher levels. These patterns were not visible in raw‑scale plots due to extreme skewness.
Group comparisons between high performers and non‑high‑performers revealed the largest separations in variables capturing elite exposure, network structure, and breadth. High performers consistently showed higher Num_Elite_Collaborators, Effective_Size, Num_Collaborators, and Num_Topics, whereas Career_Length and Cohesion_Regular displayed minimal differences. Synthesizing these insights, the strongest hypothesized predictors align with theory: elite exposure (Liu), brokerage advantages (Burt), and topic breadth (Fleming) emerge as the most influential predictors of both Log_Impact and high-performer status, and are therefore prioritized in subsequent modelling.


# Part 2: Linear Regression Analysis 


## Simple Linear Regression


```{r q6-slr}

# ================================
#  Fit Simple Regression Model
# ================================

model <- lm(Log_Impact ~ log_Num_Elite, data = df)


# ================================
# Simple Regression Model Summary
# ================================

model_summary <- summary(model)

# Extract key metrics
coef_value <- model_summary$coefficients["log_Num_Elite", "Estimate"]
p_value <- model_summary$coefficients["log_Num_Elite", "Pr(>|t|)"]
r_squared <- model_summary$r.squared

cat("===== Simple Regression Model Results =====\n")
cat("Coefficient (log_Num_Elite):", round(coef_value, 4), "\n")
cat("Simple Regression R-squared:", round(r_squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Simple Regression p-value:", format(p_value, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3), "\n")


# ================================
# Interpretation Helper
# ================================

cat("\n===== Interpretation =====\n")
cat(paste0(
  "A 1% increase in the number of elite collaborators is associated with approximately ",
  round(coef_value, 2),
  "% change in total impact (log scale interpretation).\n"
))


# ================================
# Compare with Raw Model
# ================================

model_raw <- lm(Log_Impact ~ Num_Elite_Collaborators, data = df)

cat("\n===== Simple Regression Model Comparison =====\n")
cat("Log Model R²:", round(summary(model)$r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Raw Model R²:", round(summary(model_raw)$r.squared, 4), "\n")



```

```{r q8-residuals, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}

# ================================
# Residual Diagnostics
# ================================

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model)

```

## Interpretation: Simple Linear Regression

A simple linear regression was fitted with Log_Total_Impact as the response and log(Num_Elite_Collaborators + 1) as the predictor. The estimated coefficient was 1.351, indicating a positive association between elite collaboration and impact. The model achieved an R² of 0.2887, substantially outperforming the raw-scale model (R² = 0.054), and the predictor was highly significant (p < 0.001). Interpreted in elasticity terms, a 1% increase in elite collaborators is associated with approximately a 1.35% increase in expected total impact, supporting the elite-exposure mechanism proposed by Liu et al. (2018).

Residual diagnostics showed mild curvature in the Residuals-vs-Fitted plot, suggesting some non-linearity, though no major heteroscedasticity was observed. The Q-Q plot indicated slight deviations from normality in the tails, but overall model assumptions were reasonably satisfied. These results suggest that while elite collaboration is an important predictor, additional variables and non-linear specifications may further improve model fit.

## Multiple Linear Regression

```{r q9-mlr}

# ================================
#      Fit model 
# ================================
mlr_model <- lm(Log_Impact ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length + 
              log_Num_Elite + Cohesion_Elite + log_Effective_Size, data = df)

summary(mlr_model)

```

```{r q10-vif}
# INSERT YOUR CODE for VIF analysis here
# ================================
#  Load Libraries
# ================================
library(dplyr)
library(car)
library(lmtest)


# ================================
# Coefficient Significance
# ================================
cat("\n===== Coefficient Significance =====\n")
print(round(mlr_model$coefficients, 4))

# ================================
# Multicollinearity Check (VIF)
# ================================
cat("\n===== VIF (Multicollinearity) =====\n")
vif_values <- vif(mlr_model)
print(round(vif_values, 3))

# ================================
#  Residual Diagnostics
# ================================
par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(mlr_model)

# ================================
# Independence of Residuals
# ================================
cat("\n===== Durbin-Watson Test =====\n")
print(dwtest(mlr_model))

# ================================
# Predictions
# ================================

# Log scale predictions
pred_log <- predict(mlr_model, newdata = df)

# Convert to original scale
pred_original <- exp(pred_log)

# ================================
# Model Performance
# ================================
cat("\n===== Performance (Log Scale) =====\n")
print(postResample(pred_log, df$Log_Impact))

cat("\n===== Performance (Original Scale) =====\n")
print(postResample(pred_original, df$Total_Impact))

# ================================
# Interpretation Helper
# ================================
cat("\n===== Interpretation =====\n")

coef_vals <- coef(mlr_model)

for (var in names(coef_vals)[-1]) {

  coef_value <- coef_vals[var]

  # -------------------------------
  # Case 1: log(Y) ~ log(X)
  # Elasticity: % change in Y for 1% change in X
  # -------------------------------
  if (var %in% c("log_Num_Elite", "log_Effective_Size")) {

    cat(paste0(
      "A 1% increase in ", var, 
      " is associated with approximately ",
      round(coef_value * 100, 2),
      "% change in total impact, holding other variables constant.\n"
    ))

  # -------------------------------
  # Case 2: log(Y) ~ X (non-logged)
  # Semi-elasticity: % change in Y for 1-unit increase in X
  # -------------------------------
  } else {

    pct_change <- (exp(coef_value) - 1) * 100

    cat(paste0(
      "A one-unit increase in ", var,
      " is associated with approximately ",
      round(pct_change, 2),
      "% change in total impact, holding other variables constant.\n"
    ))
  }
}

# 
```

## Interpretation: Multi Linear Regression

A multiple linear regression was estimated with log(Total_Impact) as the dependent variable and Total_Projects, Career_Length, log(Num_Elite_Collaborators + 1), Cohesion_Elite, and log(Effective_Size) as predictors. Log‑transforming the outcome addressed skewness and improved model stability. All predictors were statistically significant (p < 0.05). Model fit was moderate on the log scale (R² = 0.4599) but substantially weaker on the original scale (R² = 0.1549), confirming the appropriateness of transformation.

The largest effect was Cohesion_Elite (β = 1.181), where a one‑unit increase corresponds to a 226% rise in expected impact, reflecting a strong structural‑cohesion effect. For the log–log predictors, a 1% increase in effective network size and elite collaborators is associated with 0.78% and 0.22% increases in impact respectively. Total_Projects and Career_Length showed smaller but positive semi‑elasticities. Multicollinearity was acceptable (VIF 1.98–4.24), indicating no inflation severe enough to distort inference. The Durbin–Watson statistic (0.65) indicated positive autocorrelation, suggesting omitted non‑linear structure. Overall, the results highlight network structure and elite exposure as dominant drivers of research impact.


## Polynomial Regression


```{r q11-polynomial}

# Add squared term
df$Career_Length_sq <- df$Career_Length^2

# Fit polynomial regression
model_poly <- lm(Log_Impact ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length + Career_Length_sq +
                   log_Num_Elite + Cohesion_Elite + log_Effective_Size,
                 data = df)

summary(model_poly)

cat("\n===== Model Comparison =====\n")

cat("Multi Linear Model R²:", round(summary(mlr_model)$r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Polynomial Model R²:", round(summary(model_poly)$r.squared, 4), "\n")

cat("Multi Linear Adj R²:", round(summary(mlr_model)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Polynomial Adj R²:", round(summary(model_poly)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")



summary(model_poly)$coefficients["Career_Length_sq", ]

plot(df$Career_Length, df$Log_Impact,
     main = "Polynomial Relationship",
     xlab = "Career Length",
     ylab = "Log Impact",
     pch = 16, col = "grey")

# Add fitted curve
career_seq <- seq(min(df$Career_Length), max(df$Career_Length), length.out = 100)

pred_curve <- predict(model_poly,
  newdata = data.frame(
    Career_Length = career_seq,
    Career_Length_sq = career_seq^2,
    Total_Projects = mean(df$Total_Projects, na.rm = TRUE),
    log_Num_Elite = mean(df$log_Num_Elite, na.rm = TRUE),
    Cohesion_Elite = mean(df$Cohesion_Elite, na.rm = TRUE),
    log_Effective_Size = mean(df$log_Effective_Size, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)

lines(career_seq, pred_curve, col = "blue", lwd = 2)

```

## Standardised Coefficients


```{r q12-std-coefs}

# ================================
# Standardised Model 
# ================================
# Scale numeric predictors
df_scaled <- df %>%
  mutate(across(c(Total_Projects, Career_Length, log_Num_Elite,
                  Cohesion_Elite, log_Effective_Size),
                scale))

# Fit model with scaled predictors
model_std <- lm(Log_Impact ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length +
                  log_Num_Elite + Cohesion_Elite + log_Effective_Size,
                data = df_scaled)

summary(model_std)

# ================================
# Extract coefficients
# ================================
coef_table <- summary(model_std)$coefficients

# Remove intercept
coef_table <- coef_table[rownames(coef_table) != "(Intercept)", ]

# ================================
# Find strongest predictor
# ================================
abs_effects <- abs(coef_table[, "Estimate"])
strongest_var <- names(which.max(abs_effects))
strongest_value <- max(abs_effects)

# ================================
# Check significance of elite collaboration
# ================================
elite_p <- coef_table["log_Num_Elite", "Pr(>|t|)"]
elite_coef <- coef_table["log_Num_Elite", "Estimate"]

# ================================
# Print Interpretation
# ================================
cat("\n===== Interpretation =====\n")

cat(paste0(
  "Among all predictors, ", strongest_var,
  " has the strongest effect on Total_Impact with a coefficient of ",
  round(strongest_value, 4), 
  ", indicating it has the largest influence compared to other variables.\n"
))

cat("\n===== Effect Size Comparison =====\n")
for (var in rownames(coef_table)) {
  cat(paste0(
    var, ": Coefficient = ", round(coef_table[var, "Estimate"], 4), "\n"
  ))
}

cat("\n===== Elite Collaboration Effect =====\n")

if (elite_p < 0.05) {
  cat(paste0(
    "The effect of collaborating with elite performers (log_Num_Elite) is statistically significant (p < 0.05).\n",
    "A 1% increase in elite collaborators is associated with approximately ",
    round(elite_coef * 100, 2),
    "% increase in total impact, holding other variables constant.\n",
    "This indicates that elite collaboration has an independent and meaningful positive effect on impact.\n"
  ))
} else {
  cat("The effect of elite collaboration is not statistically significant after controlling for other variables.\n")
}
```

## Interpretation: Polynomial Regression (degree 2)

A polynomial regression including squared terms for Total_Projects and Career_Length was estimated and compared with the multiple linear regression. Model fit improved marginally (R² = 0.4623 vs. 0.4599), indicating mild non-linearity. The quadratic term is statistically significant (t = −48.62, p < 0.001), confirming a non-linear relationship. Among predictors, log_Effective_Size is the strongest determinant of Total_Impact (β = 0.7816), followed by log_Num_Elite (β = 0.1571), which implies a 1% increase in elite collaborators is associated with a 15.71% increase in impact. Cohesion_Elite also shows a meaningful effect (β = 0.3179). Overall, results suggest network structure variables dominate productivity variables in explaining research impact, with only marginal gains from non-linearity.

# Part 3: Feature Selection with LASSO


## LASSO with Cross-Validation

```{r q13-lasso}
# INSERT YOUR CODE for LASSO CV here

library(glmnet)

# Create the model matrix containing all predictors.
# model.matrix() automatically handles dummy variables and ensures a numeric matrix.
# The intercept column is removed because glmnet adds its own.
X <- model.matrix(
  ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length + log_Num_Elite +
    Cohesion_Elite + log_Effective_Size,
  data = df
)[, -1]

# Define the response variable (log-transformed Total_Impact).
y <- df$Log_Impact

# Fit a LASSO model using 10-fold cross-validation.
# alpha = 1 specifies LASSO (L1 penalty).
# standardize = TRUE ensures all predictors are placed on the same scale,
# which is essential because LASSO penalises coefficients based on magnitude.
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(
  X, y,
  alpha = 1,
  standardize = TRUE,
  nfolds = 10
)

# Extract the optimal lambda value that minimises cross-validation error.
lambda_opt <- cv_lasso$lambda.min
lambda_opt


# Extract coefficients at optimal lambda
lasso_coef <- coef(cv_lasso, s = lambda_opt)

# Convert to a clean table for reporting
coef_table <- as.matrix(lasso_coef)
coef_table <- coef_table[coef_table != 0, , drop = FALSE]   # keep only non-zero coefficients

# Identify strongest predictor (largest absolute standardised coefficient)
abs_vals <- abs(coef_table[-1, , drop = FALSE])  # remove intercept
strongest_var <- rownames(abs_vals)[which.max(abs_vals)]
strongest_value <- abs_vals[which.max(abs_vals)]

# Report strongest predictor
cat(paste0(
  "The strongest predictor selected by the LASSO model is ", strongest_var,
  ", with a coefficient of ", round(strongest_value, 4),
  ". This indicates that it has the largest influence on Log_Impact after regularisation.\n\n"
))

# Print all retained coefficients
cat("===== LASSO Coefficients at Optimal Lambda =====\n")
for (var in rownames(coef_table)) {
  cat(paste0(var, ": ", round(coef_table[var, ], 4), "\n"))
}


```

## Coefficient Path Plot

```{r q14-path, fig.width=12, fig.height=7}

# Plot the coefficient paths across the full sequence of lambda values.
# Each coloured line represents how a predictor's coefficient shrinks as lambda increases.
plot(cv_lasso$glmnet.fit, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE)
title("LASSO Coefficient Path Plot")

# Extract coefficients at optimal lambda
lasso_coef <- coef(cv_lasso, s = lambda_opt)

# Identify non-zero predictors (excluding intercept)
selected_vars <- rownames(lasso_coef)[lasso_coef[,1] != 0]
selected_vars <- selected_vars[selected_vars != "(Intercept)"]

# Print selected variables
cat("===== Variables Selected at Optimal Lambda =====\n")
for (v in selected_vars) {
  cat(paste0(v, "\n"))
}

```

## Interpretation: LASSO Regression 

A LASSO regression was fitted using log(Total_Impact) as the response and all available predictors, with 10 fold cross validation used to select the optimal penalty. The minimum MSE value occurred at λ = 0.005588, at which point LASSO retained five predictors: Total_Projects, Career_Length, log(Num_Elite_Collaborators + 1), Cohesion_Elite, and log(Effective_Size). All remaining coefficients were shrunk to zero, confirming that these variables provide the strongest independent contribution to research impact. The coefficient path plot illustrates this behaviour: under strong penalisation (left side), most coefficients collapse toward zero, while Cohesion_Elite and log(Effective_Size) remain dominant across a wide λ range. At the optimal λ, Cohesion_Elite had the largest coefficient (1.1577), followed by log(Effective_Size) (0.7827) and elite exposure (0.2273).

Cross validation MSE for LASSO was lower than the full multiple regression model, indicating improved predictive performance through regularisation. Compared with forward selection, LASSO selected an almost identical subset, reinforcing the robustness of network based predictors.


## Forward Selection Comparison


```{r q15-forward}
# INSERT YOUR CODE for forward selection comparison here
library(MASS)

# Fit the full model (all predictors)
full_model <- lm(
  Log_Impact ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length +
    log_Num_Elite + Cohesion_Elite + log_Effective_Size,
  data = df
)

# Fit the null model (intercept only)
null_model <- lm(Log_Impact ~ 1, data = df)

# Perform forward selection using AIC as the selection criterion
forward_model <- stepAIC(
  null_model,
  scope = list(lower = null_model, upper = full_model),
  direction = "forward",
  trace = FALSE
)

# Display the final selected model
summary(forward_model)

# Extract selected variables
selected_forward <- names(coef(forward_model))[-1]  # remove intercept

cat("===== Variables Selected by Forward Selection =====\n")
for (v in selected_forward) {
  cat(paste0(v, "\n"))
}

```

## Cross-Validation MSE

```{r q16-cv-mse}
# LASSO cross-validation object already created as cv_lasso
# Extract the minimum cross-validation MSE
lasso_mse <- cv_lasso$cvm[cv_lasso$lambda == cv_lasso$lambda.min]

cat("LASSO Cross-Validation MSE:", round(lasso_mse, 4), "\n")

library(caret)


# Define 10-fold CV
train_control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

# Train the full linear regression model with CV
full_cv <- train(
  Log_Impact ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length +
    log_Num_Elite + Cohesion_Elite + log_Effective_Size,
  data = df,
  method = "lm",
  trControl = train_control
)

# Extract CV MSE
full_mse <- full_cv$results$RMSE^2

cat("Full Model Cross-Validation MSE:", round(full_mse, 4), "\n")

```
## Interpretation: Forward Selection

Forward selection identified the same five predictors as LASSO: log(Effective_Size), Cohesion_Elite, Total_Projects, Career_Length, and log(Num_Elite_Collaborators + 1). The final model achieved R² = 0.46 with an identical adjusted R², indicating stable explanatory power. The F statistic was highly significant, confirming strong joint predictive ability. Cross validation MSE matched the full model (1.681), showing that forward selection did not improve predictive accuracy but produced a more parsimonious specification.

## Interpretation : Synthesis of LASSO and Forward Selection

Both LASSO and forward selection selected the same five predictors, showing strong agreement in variable importance. Crucially, the network structure variables—log(Effective_Size) and Cohesion_Elite—were consistently retained, supporting Burt’s structural holes theory that brokerage and non redundant ties enhance performance. The elite exposure variable (log_Num_Elite) also survived regularisation, aligning with Liu’s learning from stars theory. Cross validation MSE was identical across methods, indicating stable predictive accuracy. Overall, both approaches highlight network position and elite collaboration as the most robust drivers of research impact.

log_model <- glm(

```{r q19-metrics}

# -----------------------------
# Train–Test Split (70/30)
# -----------------------------
n <- nrow(df)
train_index <- sample(1:n, size = 0.7 * n)

train_data <- df[train_index, ]
test_data  <- df[-train_index, ]

# -----------------------------
# Fit Logistic Regression on Training Set
# -----------------------------
log_model <- glm(
  Is_HighPerformer ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length +
    log_Num_Elite + Cohesion_Elite + log_Effective_Size,
  data = train_data,
  family = binomial
)

# -----------------------------
# Predict on Test Set
# -----------------------------
test_prob <- predict(log_model, newdata = test_data, type = "response")
test_pred <- ifelse(test_prob > 0.5, 1, 0)

# -----------------------------
# Confusion Matrix
# -----------------------------
conf_mat <- table(
  Actual = test_data$Is_HighPerformer,
  Predicted = test_pred
)

cat("===== Confusion Matrix (Test Set) =====\n")
print(conf_mat)

# -----------------------------
# Accuracy, Precision, Recall , F1, F2
# -----------------------------
TP <- conf_mat["1", "1"]
TN <- conf_mat["0", "0"]
FP <- conf_mat["0", "1"]
FN <- conf_mat["1", "0"]

accuracy  <- (TP + TN) / sum(conf_mat)
precision <- TP / (TP + FP)
recall    <- TP / (TP + FN)

# F1 score (harmonic mean of precision & recall)
F1 <- 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall)

# F2 score (recall-weighted, penalises FN more)
F2 <- 5 * (precision * recall) / ((4 * precision) + recall)

cat("\n===== Classification Metrics =====\n")
cat(paste0("Accuracy:  ", round(accuracy, 4), "\n"))
cat(paste0("Precision: ", round(precision, 4), "\n"))
cat(paste0("Recall:    ", round(recall, 4), "\n"))
cat(paste0("F1 Score:  ", round(F1, 4), "\n"))
cat(paste0("F2 Score:  ", round(F2, 4), "\n"))

```

```{r q20-odds}

# Fit logistic regression model
 log_model <- glm(
   Is_HighPerformer ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length +
    log_Num_Elite + Cohesion_Elite + log_Effective_Size,
  data = df,
 family = binomial
)

# Extract coefficients
log_coef <- summary(log_model)$coefficients

# Report strongest predictor (largest absolute log-odds effect)
abs_vals <- abs(log_coef[-1, 1])   # exclude intercept
strongest_var <- names(abs_vals)[which.max(abs_vals)]
strongest_value <- abs_vals[which.max(abs_vals)]

cat(paste0(
  "The strongest predictor in the logistic regression model is ", strongest_var,
  ", with a log-odds coefficient of ", round(strongest_value, 4),
  ". This indicates it has the greatest influence on the probability of being a High Performer.\n\n"
))

# Print all coefficients
cat("===== Logistic Regression Coefficients =====\n")
for (v in rownames(log_coef)) {
  cat(paste0(v, ": ", round(log_coef[v, 1], 4),
             " (p = ", round(log_coef[v, 4], 4), ")\n"))
}

# Convert coefficients to odds ratios
odds_ratios <- exp(log_coef[, 1])

cat("\n===== Odds Ratios =====\n")
for (v in names(odds_ratios)) {
  cat(paste0(v, ": ", round(odds_ratios[v], 4), "\n"))
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Interpretation: Print human-readable odds statements
# -----------------------------------------------------------

cat("\n===== Interpretation of Significant Predictors =====\n")

for (v in rownames(log_coef)[-1]) {  # skip intercept
  
  coef_val <- log_coef[v, 1]
  p_val    <- log_coef[v, 4]
  OR       <- odds_ratios[v]
  
  if (p_val < 0.05) {
    direction <- ifelse(coef_val > 0, "increase", "decrease")
    
    cat(paste0(
      v, ": A one-unit increase in ", v,
      " leads to a ", round((OR - 1) * 100, 2), "% ",
      direction, " in the odds of being a high performer (OR = ",
      round(OR, 4), ").\n"
    ))
  }
}
```

## Interpretation: Logistic Regression

A logistic regression model was estimated to identify the key predictors of being classified as a High Performer. All predictors were statistically significant (p < 0.001), indicating strong explanatory power. Cohesion_Elite emerged as the most influential variable, with a log-odds coefficient of –1.7821 (OR = 0.1683), suggesting that higher elite cohesion substantially reduces the odds of high performance. This supports the view that tightly clustered elite networks may restrict access to diverse, non-redundant information. In contrast, elite exposure (log_Num_Elite) had a strong positive effect (OR = 4.3324), meaning that a 1% increase in elite collaborators is associated with a proportional increase in the odds of high performance, effectively more than tripling the odds, holding other variables constant. Total_Projects and Career_Length increased the odds by approximately 9%, while log(Effective_Size) increased the odds by 24%, highlighting the benefits of broader network reach.

Model performance was evaluated using a 70/30 train–test split with a 0.5 classification threshold. While overall accuracy was high (0.9918), more balanced metrics—precision (0.7848), recall (0.65), F1 (0.7111), and F2 (0.6731)—indicate moderate sensitivity in identifying high performers. The confusion matrix suggests strong classification of non-high performers but more conservative detection of high performers.


## Linear Discriminant Analysis(LDA)


```{r q22-lda}

# -----------------------------
# Fit LDA model
# -----------------------------
lda_model <- lda(
  Is_HighPerformer ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length +

)

# Print model summary
lda_model

# -----------------------------
# Predict on test set

lda_prob <- lda_pred$posterior[, "1"]

# Class predictions

# Confusion matrix

  Actual = test_data$Is_HighPerformer,
  Predicted = lda_class
)

# -----------------------------
# Compute metrics
# -----------------------------
TP <- conf_lda["1", "1"]
TN <- conf_lda["0", "0"]
FP <- conf_lda["0", "1"]
FN <- conf_lda["1", "0"]

accuracy  <- (TP + TN) / sum(conf_lda)
precision <- TP / (TP + FP)
recall    <- TP / (TP + FN)
F1 <- 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
F2 <- 5 * precision * recall / ((4 * precision) + recall)

cat("\n===== LDA Metrics =====\n")
cat(paste0("Accuracy:  ", round(accuracy, 4), "\n"))
cat(paste0("Precision: ", round(precision, 4), "\n"))
cat(paste0("Recall:    ", round(recall, 4), "\n"))
cat(paste0("F1 Score:  ", round(F1, 4), "\n"))
cat(paste0("F2 Score:  ", round(F2, 4), "\n"))

# Metrics function
get_metrics <- function(conf_mat) {
  TP <- conf_mat["1", "1"]
  TN <- conf_mat["0", "0"]
  FP <- conf_mat["0", "1"]
  FN <- conf_mat["1", "0"]
  
  accuracy  <- (TP + TN) / sum(conf_mat)
  precision <- TP / (TP + FP)
  recall    <- TP / (TP + FN)
  F1 <- 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
  F2 <- 5 * precision * recall / ((4 * precision) + recall)
  
  return(c(accuracy, precision, recall, F1, F2))
}

metrics_lda <- get_metrics(conf_lda)

```
## Class imbalance Analysis

```{r q25-imbalance}

# -----------------------------
# 1. Train–Test Split (70/30)
# -----------------------------
n <- nrow(df)
train_index <- sample(1:n, size = 0.7 * n)

train_data <- df[train_index, ]
test_data  <- df[-train_index, ]

# -----------------------------
# Helper function to compute metrics
# -----------------------------
get_metrics <- function(conf_mat) {
  TP <- conf_mat["1", "1"]
  TN <- conf_mat["0", "0"]
  FP <- conf_mat["0", "1"]
  FN <- conf_mat["1", "0"]
  
  accuracy  <- (TP + TN) / sum(conf_mat)
  precision <- TP / (TP + FP)
  recall    <- TP / (TP + FN)
  F1 <- 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
  F2 <- 5 * precision * recall / ((4 * precision) + recall)
  
  return(c(accuracy, precision, recall, F1, F2))
}

# ============================================================
# 2. STANDARD LOGISTIC REGRESSION
# ============================================================
log_std <- glm(
  Is_HighPerformer ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length +
    log_Num_Elite + Cohesion_Elite + log_Effective_Size,
  data = train_data,
  family = binomial
)

prob_std <- predict(log_std, newdata = test_data, type = "response")
pred_std <- ifelse(prob_std > 0.5, 1, 0)
conf_std <- table(Actual = test_data$Is_HighPerformer, Predicted = pred_std)

metrics_std <- get_metrics(conf_std)

# ============================================================
# 3. CLASS-WEIGHTED LOGISTIC REGRESSION
# ============================================================
train_data$w <- ifelse(train_data$Is_HighPerformer == 1, 20, 1)

log_w <- glm(
  Is_HighPerformer ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length +
    log_Num_Elite + Cohesion_Elite + log_Effective_Size,
  data = train_data,
  family = binomial,
  weights = w
)

prob_w <- predict(log_w, newdata = test_data, type = "response")
pred_w <- ifelse(prob_w > 0.5, 1, 0)
conf_w <- table(Actual = test_data$Is_HighPerformer, Predicted = pred_w)

metrics_w <- get_metrics(conf_w)

# ============================================================
# 4. Threshold-Tuned Logistic Regression
# ============================================================
# Threshold tuning example (0.3)
threshold <- 0.3
pred_thr <- ifelse(prob_std > threshold, 1, 0)

conf_thr <- table(
  Actual = test_data$Is_HighPerformer,
  Predicted = pred_thr
)

metrics_thr <- get_metrics(conf_thr)

cat("\n===== Metrics (Threshold = 0.3) =====\n")
print(metrics_thr)

# -----------------------------
# 5. Threshold tuning LDA (e.g., 0.3)
# -----------------------------
threshold <- 0.3
lda_class_thr <- ifelse(lda_prob > threshold, 1, 0)

# Confusion matrix
conf_lda_thr <- table(
  Actual = test_data$Is_HighPerformer,
  Predicted = lda_class_thr
)

# Metrics function
get_metrics <- function(conf_mat) {
  TP <- conf_mat["1", "1"]
  TN <- conf_mat["0", "0"]
  FP <- conf_mat["0", "1"]
  FN <- conf_mat["1", "0"]
  
  accuracy  <- (TP + TN) / sum(conf_mat)
  precision <- TP / (TP + FP)
  recall    <- TP / (TP + FN)
  F1 <- 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
  F2 <- 5 * precision * recall / ((4 * precision) + recall)
  
  return(c(accuracy, precision, recall, F1, F2))
}

metrics_lda_thr <- get_metrics(conf_lda_thr)

# ============================================================
# 5. COMBINED METRICS TABLE
# ============================================================
results <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Standard Logistic", "Weighted Logistic", "Threshold-Tuned Logistic"),
  Accuracy = round(c(metrics_std[1], metrics_w[1], metrics_thr[1]), 4),
  Precision = round(c(metrics_std[2], metrics_w[2], metrics_thr[2]), 4),
  Recall = round(c(metrics_std[3], metrics_w[3], metrics_thr[3]), 4),
  F1 = round(c(metrics_std[4], metrics_w[4], metrics_thr[4]), 4),
  F2 = round(c(metrics_std[5], metrics_w[5], metrics_thr[5]), 4)
)

cat("\n===== MODEL COMPARISON TABLE =====\n")
print(results)
```

## Interpretation: LDA and Class Imbalance address 

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) was applied to classify High Performers in a dataset with extreme class imbalance (only 1.4% high performers). Because LDA does not support class weights directly, class imbalance was addressed using prior probabilities, which adjust the classification boundary to reflect the rarity of high performers. In the broader modelling pipeline, class weighted logistic regression and threshold tuning were also used to counter imbalance, ensuring fairer evaluation of minority class predictions.

The LDA priors (0.984 for class 0; 0.016 for class 1) shift the model toward identifying rare high performers. Group means show strong separation: high performers have substantially higher Total_Projects, Career_Length, log_Num_Elite, Cohesion_Elite, and log_Effective_Size. The LDA coefficients highlight log_Num_Elite (1.817) and Cohesion_Elite (–2.303) as the strongest discriminants, reinforcing earlier findings that elite exposure and network structure are key drivers of performance.
On the test set, LDA achieved Accuracy = 0.9893, Precision = 0.6254, and Recall = 0.7961, with an F2 score of 0.7549, showing strong sensitivity to high performers. Threshold tuned LDA further improved recall to 0.8185, outperforming both standard and weighted logistic models.

Overall, LDA demonstrates strong capability in detecting minority class high performers, confirming the importance of network structure and elite collaboration.

```{r q27-cohesion}

# ============================

# ============================

interaction_coef <- coef(summary(log_interaction))["log_Num_Elite:Cohesion_Elite", ]

  cat("\nConclusion: The interaction is statistically SIGNIFICANT.\n")
} else {
  cat("\nConclusion: The interaction is NOT statistically significant.\n")
}

library(interactions)

cat("\n===== Plotting Interaction Effect =====\n")
interact_plot(
  log_interaction,
  pred = log_Num_Elite,
  modx = Cohesion_Elite,
  plot.points = FALSE
)

library(margins)

cat("\n===== Marginal Effects for Interaction Model =====\n")
marginal_effects <- margins(log_interaction)
print(summary(marginal_effects))


```
```{r  Cohesion_Elite vs. Cohesion_Regular}

# ============================================================
# Fit logistic regression with both cohesion variables
# ============================================================

log_compare <- glm(
  Is_HighPerformer ~ Total_Projects + Career_Length +
    log_Num_Elite + Cohesion_Elite + Cohesion_Regular + log_Effective_Size,
  data = df,
  family = binomial
)

cat("\n===== Logistic Regression: Cohesion_Elite vs Cohesion_Regular =====\n")
print(summary(log_compare))


# ============================================================
# Extract coefficients for both cohesion variables
# ============================================================

coef_table <- coef(summary(log_compare))[c("Cohesion_Elite", "Cohesion_Regular"), ]

cat("\n===== Coefficients for Cohesion Variables =====\n")
cat("Cohesion_Elite:\n")
cat("  Estimate:   ", round(coef_table["Cohesion_Elite", "Estimate"], 5), "\n")
cat("  Std.Error:  ", round(coef_table["Cohesion_Elite", "Std. Error"], 5), "\n")
cat("  z-value:    ", round(coef_table["Cohesion_Elite", "z value"], 5), "\n")
cat("  p-value:    ", round(coef_table["Cohesion_Elite", "Pr(>|z|)"], 5), "\n\n")

cat("Cohesion_Regular:\n")
cat("  Estimate:   ", round(coef_table["Cohesion_Regular", "Estimate"], 5), "\n")
cat("  Std.Error:  ", round(coef_table["Cohesion_Regular", "Std. Error"], 5), "\n")
cat("  z-value:    ", round(coef_table["Cohesion_Regular", "z value"], 5), "\n")
cat("  p-value:    ", round(coef_table["Cohesion_Regular", "Pr(>|z|)"], 5), "\n")


# ============================================================
# Significance statements
# ============================================================

cat("\n===== Significance Assessment =====\n")

if (coef_table["Cohesion_Elite", "Pr(>|z|)"] < 0.05) {
  cat("Cohesion_Elite is SIGNIFICANT.\n")
} else {
  cat("Cohesion_Elite is NOT significant.\n")
}

if (coef_table["Cohesion_Regular", "Pr(>|z|)"] < 0.05) {
  cat("Cohesion_Regular is SIGNIFICANT.\n")
} else {
  cat("Cohesion_Regular is NOT significant.\n")
}


# ============================================================
# Odds ratios for interpretation
# ============================================================

odds_ratios <- exp(coef(log_compare)[c("Cohesion_Elite", "Cohesion_Regular")])

cat("\n===== Odds Ratios =====\n")
cat("Cohesion_Elite OR:   ", round(odds_ratios["Cohesion_Elite"], 5), "\n")
cat("Cohesion_Regular OR: ", round(odds_ratios["Cohesion_Regular"], 5), "\n")


# ============================================================
# Final interpretation summary
# ============================================================

cat("\n===== Interpretation Summary =====\n")

if (coef_table["Cohesion_Elite", "Estimate"] < 0) {
  cat("Cohesion_Elite has a NEGATIVE effect on high-performer likelihood.\n")
} else {
  cat("Cohesion_Elite has a POSITIVE effect on high-performer likelihood.\n")
}

if (coef_table["Cohesion_Regular", "Estimate"] < 0) {
  cat("Cohesion_Regular has a NEGATIVE effect on high-performer likelihood.\n")
} else {
  cat("Cohesion_Regular has a POSITIVE effect on high-performer likelihood.\n")
}

cat("\nComparison complete.\n")


```
## Intepretation: Interaction and Cohesion_Elite vs. Cohesion_Regular

The results show a clear divergence between elite and regular cohesion in predicting high‑performer status. Cohesion_Elite has a strong positive effect (β = 1.899, OR = 6.68), indicating that tighter integration with elite collaborators substantially increases the likelihood of high performance. In contrast, Cohesion_Regular has a large negative effect (β = –8.10, OR = 0.0003), meaning dense ties among non‑elite collaborators dramatically reduce performance odds. The significant interaction term (log_Num_Elite × Cohesion_Elite, β = –1.508) shows that elite cohesion amplifies the benefits of elite exposure but weakens when cohesion becomes excessive. Importantly, the two cohesion variables have opposite signs exactly as Liu et al. (2018) predict, reinforcing the theoretical distinction between elite and regular network structures.

## Interpretation: FINAL SYNTHESIS: ADVICE FOR BECOMING A HIGH PERFORMER 

Across all models, three predictors consistently explain star emergence: elite exposure, network diversity, and elite cohesion dynamics. log_Num_Elite is the strongest and most stable predictor, while Effective_Size highlights the value of broad, non‑redundant networks. Cohesion_Elite and Cohesion_Regular show opposite signs, aligning with Liu et al. (2018) and reinforcing that elite and non‑elite structures operate differently. Overall, the data most strongly supports Burt’s structural‑holes theory, with Liu’s elite‑learning mechanism also validated; Fleming’s breadth theory receives partial support but is less dominant. Limitations include the inability to measure knowledge flows directly, potential omitted‑variable bias, and assumptions of linearity and independence that may not fully hold in networked data. Practically, the evidence suggests a clear strategy: build ties to elite collaborators, expand network diversity, avoid overly cohesive elite clusters, and maintain moderate cohesion with regular collaborators. Threshold‑tuned LDA remains the most effective model for detecting emerging stars.



# Code Explanation

The analysis began with data loading and preprocessing, where the dataset was imported using standard R functions such as read.csv(). Initial checks included verifying variable types, inspecting summary statistics, and identifying missing values. NA handling was performed using listwise deletion because the proportion of missingness was extremely small and not systematically related to the outcome. This avoided introducing bias through imputation and ensured compatibility with modelling functions such as glmnet and lda.

Several variables were log‑transformed, including Total_Impact and Num_Elite_Collaborators. These transformations were chosen because the raw distributions were highly right‑skewed, violating linearity assumptions in regression and inflating leverage. Log‑transformation stabilised variance, improved normality, and produced more interpretable multiplicative effects. This also aligns with prior literature on scientific productivity, where impact and collaboration counts typically follow power‑law distributions.

For the LASSO regression, the glmnet package was used with 10‑fold cross‑validation via cv.glmnet(). Ten folds represent a widely accepted balance between computational efficiency and variance reduction. LASSO was selected because it performs variable selection and shrinkage simultaneously, addressing multicollinearity among network variables. The optimal λ was chosen using the minimum‑MSE rule, ensuring the best out‑of‑sample predictive performance. Coefficient path plots were generated to visualise how predictors entered or exited the model as regularisation increased.

The forward selection model was implemented using stepAIC() and compared directly with LASSO. This allowed assessment of whether classical stepwise procedures converge on similar predictors. Both methods selected nearly identical variables, reinforcing the robustness of the findings.

For logistic regression, the full model was estimated using glm(family = binomial). Odds ratios were computed using exp(coef()) to provide interpretable effect sizes. Because the dataset exhibited extreme class imbalance (only 1.4% high performers), a 70/30 train–test split was used to evaluate generalisation. This split is standard in predictive modelling and ensures sufficient minority‑class representation in both sets. Additional imbalance‑handling methods included class‑weighted logistic regression (via weights=) and threshold tuning, where the classification cutoff was adjusted to maximise recall and F2 score. These methods were necessary because standard logistic regression tends to predict the majority class overwhelmingly.

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) was implemented using MASS::lda(). LDA incorporates prior probabilities, which naturally adjust for class imbalance. Threshold‑tuned LDA was also evaluated by shifting the posterior probability cutoff. Confusion matrices, accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and F2 scores were computed using custom functions and caret::confusionMatrix().

ROC curves were generated using pROC::roc() and plotted to compare ranking performance across models. ROC analysis confirmed that all models had strong discriminative ability, with threshold‑tuned LDA and logistic regression performing best for minority‑class detection.

Several difficulties were encountered. First, mismatched datasets caused errors when comparing models; this was resolved by ensuring all models used the same filtered dataset. Second, LASSO required matrix inputs, so categorical variables were encoded using model.matrix(). Third, class imbalance caused unstable recall values, which was addressed through weighting and threshold tuning. Finally, interpreting interaction terms required centering variables to reduce multicollinearity.

Overall, the code pipeline ensured reproducibility, theoretical alignment, and robust model comparison across multiple statistical frameworks.

## A.3: Misclassification Profile


```{r appendix-classification}
# Misclassification Profile

# Compute probabilities on df_small
probs <- predict(log_model, newdata = df_small, type = "response")

# Assign safely
df_small$prob <- probs

# Now classification works
df_small$pred_class <- ifelse(df_small$prob > 0.5, 1, 0)

df_small$pred_class <- ifelse(df_small$prob > 0.5, 1, 0)

df_small$err_type <- case_when(
  df_small$pred_class == 1 & df_small$Is_HighPerformer == 0 ~ "False Positive",
  df_small$pred_class == 0 & df_small$Is_HighPerformer == 1 ~ "False Negative",
  TRUE ~ "Correct"
)

ggplot(df_small, aes(log_Num_Elite, Cohesion_Elite, colour = err_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Misclassification Profile",
       colour = "Error Type")

```
